newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan tries to broker Afghan truce.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan tries to broker Afghan truce.

text.p: Pakistan is mediating between Afghanistan's new Islamic Taleban rulers and northern Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum to prevent any military showdown, a Pakistani foreign ministry official said on Monday.
"So far they are not agreeing to talk to each other," said the official, who asked not to be named.
A delegation from Dostum's mainly Uzbek Jumbish-i-Milli faction was in the Pakistani city of Peshawar, but had not proceeded to Kabul to meet Taleban leaders, he said.
Pakistan has denied accusations that it supports the Taleban, saying it has no favourites among Afghan factions.
The official said Dostum, who controls six northern provinces, wanted to be recognised as an "equal partner" by the Taleban and left alone to govern his territory.
The Taleban were saying they were now the central government and wanted to control the whole of Afghanistan, he said.

The official said Pakistan's efforts to mediate between the Taleban and Dostum, whose forces face each other near the vital Salang Tunnel 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, were running on similar lines to those of U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl.
"The only difference is that Holl is trying to promote wider national reconciliation, while we are focusing on preventing a conflict between Dostum and the Taleban," the official said.
Holl has been shuttling between Kabul and Dostum's territory in an effort to head off a military confrontation.

A Pakistani delegation left Islamabad on Sunday for a rapid swing through Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan aimed at convincing leaders of the Central Asian states bordering Afghanistan that the Taleban had no designs on their territory.
"We don't see the Taleban crossing into Central Asia," the foreign ministry official said. "They are an indigenous movement that is concerned with internal Afghan affairs."
Russia and the Central Asian states have voiced concern at the swift rise to power of the Islamic militants, who seized Kabul from ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani on September 27.

Pakistani President Farooq Leghari is due to visit the Central Asian states of Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan later this month, with events in Afghanistan likely to be at the top of his agenda, the foreign ministry official said.
"He will also be discussing how we can develop communication links, such as roads and pipelines, from Central Asia to Pakistan across Afghanistan," he said.
Leghari is scheduled to visit the Uzbek capital Tashkent from October 18 to 20. He will visit Kyrgyzstan from October 25 to 28 and Kazakhstan from October 28 to 30.

In Kabul, acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammed Ghous said on Monday that Dostum appeared to be ready to back ex-government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, now battling to keep Taleban fighters out of his Panjsher Valley base north of Kabul.
The British Broadcasting Corporation quoted Dostum as saying he would come to the aid of any compatriot under attack unless the Taleban stopped fighting, an apparent reference to Masood.

"Now it seems that they are interested in joining together to take action against the Taleban. If General Dostum realises this aim, it will be a great mistake," said Ghous, whose government has said it has no quarrel with Dostum.

He called on Dostum and Masood to accept a general amnesty offer and assured Masood, widely regarded as one of the best guerrilla commanders in the war against the Soviet-backed government in the 1980s, that he would not be harmed if he surrendered.
"Nothing would put his life in jeopardy and he can take part in the future government," Ghous told reporters.
